title: Grok vs. Dot vs. Muse vs. Claude Duet: Nine Tasks, Four Agents, No Universal Winner
summary: Claire Vo puts four personal agents through nine real tasks. Grok Bot wins the broad work test, Muse handles personal and creative jobs, and the coding favorites expose the limits of an overall score.
body:
Grok vs. Dot vs. Muse vs. Claude Duet: Nine Tasks, Four Agents, No Universal Winner
Claire Vo puts four personal agents through nine real tasks. Grok Bot wins the broad work test, Muse handles personal and creative jobs, and the coding favorites expose the limits of an overall score.
Claire Vo
Watch or listen to the full episode
Episode chapters
6 chapters
- 2:14Building the benchmark and checking agent accessClaire selects nine real tasks, uses computer-use operators, and explains the setup differences that limit the comparison.
- 10:11Slack replies, short clips, and bug fixesDot understands Claire’s preferences, Muse produces the strongest short clip, and coding review reveals a risky validation change.
- 17:31Figma thumbnails and actionable inbox triageGrok wins on new thumbnail ideas and a document interface that makes to-dos easier to use.
- 20:49Family newspapers, homework, and shoe shoppingMuse excels at family-oriented artifacts and fast explanations; Grok handles product comparison best.
- 26:25A launch video reverses Claude’s video-editing failureClaude Duet follows the product brief, branding, and voiceover workflow better than the other agents.
- 30:14Final ranking and which agent to useGrok leads the overall ranking, Muse stands out for personal tasks, and Claire separates personal agents from her preferred coding tools.
Workflows from this episode
- Create a Personalized Family Newspaper with Meta's Muse
- How to Create a Branded Product Launch Video with Claude Duet
- Generate Novel YouTube Thumbnail Ideas with Grok and Figma
All workflows
Episode outline
Claude Duet wouldn’t download a video to cut a short clip. Later, it made the best product launch video in the entire test, complete with branding and an ElevenLabs voiceover.
That contradiction is more useful than a leaderboard. “Make a video” sounds like one capability until you ask an agent to find footage, download it, choose cuts, follow a design skill, or generate narration. Different jobs expose different strengths—and very different failure modes.
I ran Dot, Grok Bot, Muse, and Claude Duet through nine tasks I actually need done. Grok won the overall ranking. Muse was my favorite for several personal and creative tasks. Dot and Duet did the strongest coding work, but that didn’t make either my preferred general-purpose assistant.
I wanted to know which agent could finish a useful piece of work without making me manage every step.
A benchmark built around my actual work—and imperfect access
I started by asking each agent for the top 10 tasks it does for me. Then I put those lists into Claude and asked it to build a benchmark around the most common tasks, while testing different capabilities.
The benchmark covered nine jobs I actually needed done:
- Draft a Slack reply.
- Cut a short-form video.
- Fix a Sentry bug.
- Make a How I AI thumbnail.
- Triage my inbox.
- Build a family newspaper.
- Explain a physics question to my fourth grader.
- Shop for shoes.
- Make a ChatPRD Product Intelligence launch video.
I wanted lightweight prompts, written the way I would actually ask for help. My instruction during preparation was: “Keep it in my voice. Do exactly what I would do.” The run sheet included each prompt, responses to likely follow-up questions, and ways to nudge a stalled agent. This wasn’t a competition in elaborate prompt engineering.
Then I used agents to operate the agents. Claude ComputerUse ran Dot; Codex operated Grok Bot, Muse, and Claude Duet. Running tasks in parallel was genuinely useful. The operator layer was less reliable: computer use broke, I had to intervene, and I was particularly frustrated with Claude ComputerUse.
I also had Codex use BrowserUse to check connections and skills. That is worth copying even if you never run a benchmark. When several agents have different email accounts and connectors, apparent differences in intelligence can really be differences in access.
And I still missed things. Muse didn’t have Slack or GitHub connected. Claude only had my work calendar for the family newspaper. Existing memories differed, and using different operator agents introduced another variable.
So this was a practical comparison of my setups, not a controlled model evaluation. I judged the outputs openly, recorded my reactions, and gave that transcript to Claude for the final ranking. The reported 93% for Grok and 79% for Duet came from that scoring process; I did not establish a transparent scoring formula. Treat them as summaries of this run, not portable performance statistics.
Grok’s work advantage was often the artifact, not the answer
The Slack reply was a useful example of why “sounds like me” and “acts in my interests” are different criteria.
A friend at Lovable had asked me to give a talk. The agents with access produced broadly acceptable replies. Grok sounded most like me. Dot, however, asked whether the event was remote and whether I would be paid. Those are material details for someone with a busy schedule who prefers not to leave the house.
Dot understood the decision better, even if the writing task itself wasn’t difficult. Muse couldn’t participate because I hadn’t connected Slack; that was a setup failure, not evidence that it couldn’t draft a reply.
Inbox triage exposed a different distinction. The agents generally found reasonable things to do. Grok delivered them in a Grok document: organized, readable, and equipped with check marks. Claude wanted to use its task follow-up list. Muse, working from Gmail, found parenting obligations ahead of Halloween week. Dot returned a message with roughly five priorities.
For me, Grok’s document was the best working surface. A list buried in a chat message creates more work than an artifact I can actually use. This is why Grok Bot functions as my chief of staff: the interface matters after the reasoning is finished.
Grok also won the thumbnail task. We already had good templates and a Figma MCP connection, so the agents weren’t starting from a blank canvas. Dot and Claude successfully put new content into existing templates. Grok produced new headline and thumbnail ideas that I liked. Muse made a composition with Blair peeking through what looked like creepy curtains. That one was a clear rejection.
The shopping test reinforced Grok’s advantage in navigation and comparison. I wanted red Adidas Tokyos at a good price. Grok found good options; Muse came close with some steering. Claude repeatedly encountered blocked shopping sites, searched for white shoes with red stripes rather than red shoes with white stripes, and found the most expensive options. Dot barely compared alternatives.
If you’re adapting these tasks, my recommendation is to define the usable output: an actionable checklist, a thumbnail candidate, or a comparison of the correct product and color. That makes it harder to mistake a plausible response for a completed job.
Muse won the short clip—and the family newspaper
For the short-form video, the agents had access to a transcript and raw footage from our episode with Blair from Reddit. The job was to find the footage in Dropbox, download it, and cut a clip. I didn’t manually edit the results.
Claude Duet wouldn’t download the video, so it failed before editing began. The other three produced clips, but their choices differed enough to make the winner obvious.
The three clips each had a different problem or strength:
- Grok handled zooming better, but its overlays were ugly; one landed on Blair’s forehead.
- Dot’s clip looked good but lacked punchy cuts.
- Muse used a simple How I AI tag, a familiar caption layout, and stronger pacing. It didn’t have the zoom effects, but I preferred its clip.
Muse won a task I hadn’t previously used it for. I had already been using it to post social content; this result gave me a reason to consider it for creating that content too. A better skill might improve these outputs further, but that was an opportunity to test later, not something this run proved.
The family newspaper made the same preference more pronounced. This is something I print for my kids: the week’s schedule, reminders, weather, and interesting news. I already run a version through my Grok bot, TradBot.
Grok made a useful paper with school information, a “don’t forget” list, Bay Area sports, Halloween content, and weather. Muse made the most appealing family artifact: an illustrated header, a schedule on one page, and day-by-day weather, ideas, and inspiration on a second. It took two pages, which I was happy to accept because the result was inviting.
Dot’s design was poor. Claude produced a Markdown outline after finding it lacked the relevant calendar access. That limitation was real, but instructions for making a newspaper were not the newspaper I had requested.
For readers copying this workflow, the adaptation is straightforward: connect the relevant family information and specify a printable artifact. Then inspect it before printing. A cute layout does not verify a schedule, and the episode’s review focused heavily on presentation rather than an item-by-item accuracy audit.
Muse also won the homework explanation on speed. All four agents correctly answered a velocity-over-time question—the answer was C—and explained it adequately. Muse responded in approximately half a second, by my observation; it was too fast to capture in the timing record. When correctness was effectively tied, responsiveness determined which tool I wanted to use again.
Coding exposed the danger of a fast, plausible fix
The coding task started with a bug from Sentry. Muse couldn’t work on it because I hadn’t given it GitHub access. When I suggested assigning it to Devin in Linear, it interpreted Devin as a person rather than an agent.
The other agents took about 10 minutes. I then had what I described in the review as Claude Opus 5.5 grade their fixes.
Dot, using Codex, came closest to the intended fix. Claude Duet found a second bug and also recognized that Dot had already fixed the original issue, concluding it didn’t need to ship more code for that part. That restraint mattered: generating another change is not inherently better than recognizing existing work.
Grok’s fix was the concerning one. It loosened validation, effectively avoiding the problem by accepting something that should have been rejected. It was fast, but speed didn’t make the change correct.
This was a win for Dot and Duet, with extra credit to Claude for the additional bug. It was also a reminder that the overall winner should not automatically get repository access and responsibility for shipping code.
My practical recommendation remains narrower than “use these personal agents to code.” I would use the underlying coding tools—Codex and Claude—directly. Review still needs to establish whether a patch preserves the requirement, rather than simply making an error disappear.
Claude’s launch video redeemed a very uneven run
The last task was a launch video for Product Intelligence, a feature I was working on for ChatPRD. Unlike the short clip, this task had an existing skill intended to guide the output.
Dot produced something closer to a soothing PowerPoint than the launch video I wanted. Grok followed my skill and produced a recognizable version of our video style, but with layout problems and overflowing content.
Muse lacked access to my repository, so I had not set it up to succeed. It nevertheless produced an ambitious video with a British-accented overview—and made things up. The production effort did not compensate for missing product grounding.
Claude Duet delivered the most complete result. It captured the value proposition, used our branding, and avoided the layout problems. It also asked to use the ElevenLabs MCP and generated a voiceover. I would have preferred a female voice, or my own recorded voice in ElevenLabs, but the underlying artifact was clearly the best.
That is the distinction worth retaining: Claude failed at downloading and cutting an existing

title: Inside Figma’s PM OS: 31 AI Skills, Better Bug Bashes, and an Automated Growth Loop
summary: Figma product manager Ezra Mechaber shows Claire Vo how a lightweight repo became an internal PM operating system—and where browser agents, automated experiments, and a real-time writing assistant still need human judgment.
body:
Inside Figma’s PM OS: 31 AI Skills, Better Bug Bashes, and an Automated Growth Loop
Figma product manager Ezra Mechaber shows Claire Vo how a lightweight repo became an internal PM operating system—and where browser agents, automated experiments, and a real-time writing assistant still need human judgment.
Featuring Ezra Mechaber · Product Manager at Figma
Claire Vo
Watch or listen to the full episode
Episode chapters
6 chapters
- 2:05Building PM OS to raise the floorWhy Ezra started with forgotten tasks, stakeholder context, and baseline PM work.
- 10:38Inside the repo and shared skillsThe repo structure, private workspaces, adoption process, artifacts, FigJam generation, and coaching.
- 17:43Browser-based bug bashingUsing Codex and FigJam test plans to exercise complex flows and report edge cases.
- 22:28Auto XP’s experiment loopSlack-triggered Cursor automations coordinate analysis, UX writing, and engineering around a human review gate.
- 27:20A real-time writing assistant with JevA prototype checks unfinished thoughts and retrieves supporting material when the writer pauses.
- 34:09Personal agents and poisoned contextInstinct, everyday delegation, and why restarting a conversation can beat arguing with an agent.
Workflows from this episode
- Build a Personal PM Operating System with a Shared Knowledge Repo
- Build an Automated Growth Experiment Loop with Multiple AI Agents
- Automate Software Bug Bashing with a Browser Agent
All workflows
Episode outline
An AI bug bash found that putting 1,000 emojis into a text box could break it. It also caught something less spectacular and easier to ship: Figma’s seat-request copy used “a” where a particular team name required “an.”
Neither bug was glamorous, but both were easy to miss in a rushed test.
That bug bash says a lot about Ezra Mechaber’s approach to AI. A product manager at Figma, Ezra helped build an internal PM OS with 31 skills, then pushed into browser-based testing, automated growth experiments, and a writing assistant that checks your work whenever you stop typing. The ambition gets big. The starting point is deliberately modest: do the necessary work that otherwise gets skipped.
These are internal and individual workflows Ezra describes, not official Figma products. And their maturity varies: the PM OS is a shared working setup, the experiment loop is still approaching its intended operating model, and the writing assistant is a prototype whose live demo encounters an access constraint. They are at very different stages.
The useful part of a PM operating system is its context
Ezra’s original goal was to be “lazy in the right places.” He wasn’t looking for another way to generate more documents. He wanted help with jobs he did poorly or forgot entirely: looping support into a launch, taking meeting notes, finding the person who owns a piece of the product.
At a company of roughly 2,000 people, knowing who should review a decision is real work. Figma had several org-chart tools, Ezra says, but they weren’t stitched together usefully. PM OS added a skill for questions such as “who owns X?” and used that context while writing documents. A PM shouldn’t have to repeatedly explain that Charlotte is their designer and Aman is their engineering manager just to get the right reviewers included.
Claire’s framing is useful here: AI should “raise the floor” as well as “take off the ceiling.” Remembering to involve support may be less glamorous than generating a prototype, but it removes a predictable failure from the team’s operating system.
The implementation is a basic repo. It began in Claude Code as a terminal user interface and includes:
- An agents.md file describing how the assistant should behave.
- A memory file and context about the PM and their collaborators.
- Modular skills describing when to activate and what to do.
- Command hooks, including a startup check for a newer PM OS version.
- A shared template and a private workspace for each PM.
The workspace arrangement uses two Git repos: a shared parent repo and a per-PM workspace as a sub-repo, allowing people to write work back privately. A hidden dot-folder holds the base template context. The machinery was partly a practical accommodation for getting roughly 60–70 PMs, including people new to GitHub, onto a common setup.
Ezra’s most frequently used skill is “What’s Up,” which he says he runs about six times a day. It pulls together relevant Slack channels and projects, outstanding decisions, and things he owes other people. The instructions tell it which channels matter and to read whole threads rather than isolated messages.
That last detail is worth copying. A briefing is only useful if it can distinguish a new request from a request already resolved ten messages later.
The caveat: Ezra tried to build a benchmark and wasn’t successful. He doesn’t know how much this tailored setup now outperforms a vanilla agent. As models improve, he has been removing instructions that no longer earn their place. Treat the repo as maintained operating context, not a permanent monument to prompt engineering.
Adoption meant leaving the terminal—and pruning the skills
PM OS started with Ezra, Jinan, and Lawrence trading PRs in a small Slack channel. The initial explosion of skills was followed by editing. At a spring offsite, Figma’s PMs installed it, used it, modified it, and were invited to roast it.
The roasting helped the team decide which skills were worth keeping.
There is no usage telemetry. Ezra chose not to instrument it partly because he didn’t want people to feel watched and partly because this was work done on the side. Feedback came through conversation and a public channel; engineering managers began using it, and data scientists developed what he describes as essentially a fork. That supports a story of internal interest, not a measured productivity claim.
Some skills produce artifacts rather than briefings. “Build artifact” uses HTML and CSS templates plus an internal hosting tool to create and publish small presentations or dashboards. Ezra’s dashboard for this episode was one such artifact. Another PM built a FigJam builder using Figma’s MCP to generate workshop templates, with instructions reflecting the team’s visual preferences.
The coaching skill takes a different set of inputs: a career ladder, feedback, prior experiences, and a current problem. Ezra uses it for a first pass at his own coaching before taking the issue to someone else. Its value is partly in recalling patterns—for example, that a previous conflict with a colleague turned out to be a misunderstanding after a conversation.
That is useful preparation for human advice. It is not independent evidence about a colleague’s motives.
The interface also changed. Reading and writing in a terminal’s monospace text was unpleasant, so the team built a local browser front end with Markdown formatting and mobile support. Ezra now says he works in Codex essentially all the time, particularly because browser use has improved. The durable investment was the context and skills, not loyalty to the original interface.
Give the browser agent a test plan, not a vague assignment
Ezra’s team writes a FigJam test plan for an upcoming experiment or redesign. It spells out:
- The test account to use.
- The path to follow.
- The actions to take.
- What to inspect.
He gives himself one account and the agent, Astra, another. In a persistent Codex conversation, he asks it to follow the documented scenarios in the browser. When it finishes, it writes its findings back to the FigJam board.
The example involved simplifying Figma’s request modals. The interface changes were mostly UX and writing, but the underlying logic was complex. Ezra’s instruction was to keep working through the specified scenarios rather than stopping after a quick pass.
The 1,000-emoji failure and the team-name article error were findings he reported from the preceding month, rather than bugs discovered live during the episode. They illustrate different benefits: stress-testing an input and exercising a copy variation dependent on account data.
The remaining annoyance is output quality. The team is still tuning the comments so the agent’s contributions aren’t irritating. Finding something useful and reporting it usefully are separate jobs.
To adapt this approach, start with an executable test plan:
- An appropriate test account.
- Explicit steps and expected behavior.
- A shared place for findings.
Keep a human responsible for deciding which findings block launch. This checklist is an adaptation of Ezra’s setup.
Auto XP compresses the experiment handoff, but keeps a review gate
“As a growth PM,” Ezra says, “the biggest sin you can commit is wasting traffic.” His next project, Auto XP, asks whether agents can run experiments on surfaces the team would otherwise never prioritize.
The system uses three Cursor automations triggered through Slack. Auto XP has its own channel, and each stage writes back into the same thread so someone can follow the experiment’s progress.
A starting request can be as loose as:
“Hey, Auto XP, go find an experiment to run on our settings page. See what you can do. Go crazy.”
Behind that casual request are three agent automations:
- A data scientist examines drop-off, funnels, and mix shift.
- A UX writer proposes copy.
- An engineering agent picks up the implementation and PR.
Ezra says the team is moving toward more front-end design work as well.
The intended human checkpoint comes before launch: review the data science findings, hypothesis, UX writing, and code together. When the experiment finishes, a webhook triggers analysis and instructions guide whether to explore further, exploit a result, or treat it as a win or loss. The next iteration can then begin.
This is where the distinction between goal and current operation is essential. Ezra calls the theory great and the practice “almost there.” Engineer Marion has been pushing it forward. At the time of the conversation, Ezra reports five concurrent live experiments on work the team would not otherwise have done, and a “huge win” from the first experiment. He does not provide a lift figure, metric, or statistical detail.
The result worth taking seriously is the expansion of what the team can test. The result we cannot independently evaluate is the size or reliability of that first win.
My adaptation would be to preserve the human gate and define experiment eligibility before expanding autonomy. Ezra’s system draws on his accumulated growth-PM instructions; it is not evidence that any team can delegate experimental judgment to a generic agent.
A writing assistant that waits for you to pause
Ezra’s final prototype uses Jev, which he describes as a cheap, fast model that can answer constrained questions with outputs such as a number, a boolean, or a multiple-choice selection.
Instead of asking a large model to continuously rewrite a document, he makes a call whenever the writer stops typing. The check looks for blanks, unfinished thoughts, and claims worth supporting. The assistant can then consult a supplied library for relevant material.
During the demo, a recent move of the API behind an internal firewall initially interferes with execution. Later, Ezra shows the intended behavior with two examples. A sentence ending in “TK” is recognized as unfinished, but the assistant says it cannot know what he intended because the answer is absent from the library. A sentence beginning “We spoke with X writers and they said…” triggers retrieval of interview quotes from the example library.
That contrast is the interesting part. Detecting a hole is different from having evidence to fill it. The prototype’s useful behavior includes admitting the library cannot supply the missing thought. Retrieved quotes still require the writer to verify that they support the claim being made.
The verdict: copy the context layer and the documented browser bug bash first. They are especially suited t

title: Claude Duet Is Beautiful. That Doesn’t Make It My Go-To Agent.
summary: Claire tests Anthropic’s Claude Duet on inbox triage, Warriors tickets, sales work, and a launch video. The design stands out; slow responses, weak follow-through, and missing desktop and team support make it harder to keep using.
body:
Claude Duet Is Beautiful. That Doesn’t Make It My Go-To Agent.
Claire tests Anthropic’s Claude Duet on inbox triage, Warriors tickets, sales work, and a launch video. The design stands out; slow responses, weak follow-through, and missing desktop and team support make it harder to keep using.
Claire Vo
Watch or listen to the full episode
Episode chapters
6 chapters
- 0:00Personal agent fatigue and the bar for DuetClaire explains why another personal agent needs to be exceptional to earn a place in her working stack.
- 0:35Onboarding, connections, artifacts, and channelsA walkthrough of Duet’s mobile experience and the design choices that make it stand out.
- 5:20Proactivity, inbox triage, and Warriors ticketsEarly tasks reveal weak prioritization and follow-up that does not reliably bring Claire back to the work.
- 7:48Latency and the missing desktop handoffLong-running threads and a disconnected desktop experience make Duet harder to use as a daily coworker.
- 11:50Sales work and the local skills gapConnected business data helps with sales tasks, but deck design and launch-video skills do not carry over as expected.
- 14:01Team sharing and the final verdictClaire weighs Duet’s single-player design against the needs of a small team and explains why it has not become her primary agent.
Workflows from this episode
- How to Draft a Sales Deck on Your Phone Using Claude Duet
- Analyze Your Sales Pipeline Using Claude Duet's Connected Apps
All workflows
Episode outline
Claude Duet kept track of the work I gave it. I still forgot about the work.
That is the tension in Anthropic’s new personal agent. It has thoughtful onboarding, task lists, artifacts, and a genuinely polished mobile interface. But when I sent it off to find Warriors tickets, the task took long enough—and the follow-up was quiet enough—that I moved on. A checklist showing that an agent is working is useful. It is not the same as getting me to a decision.
I have personal agent fatigue. I use enough of these products that a new one has to earn its place against tools already embedded in my day. Being well designed gets my attention. Closing loops is what keeps it.
This was an early-access test of Claude Duet, while the product was in research preview. My experience is a snapshot, not a claim that its limitations are permanent. But the test surfaced a practical question: can a beautifully designed agent become a reliable coworker if I keep forgetting to return to it?
The interface gets the important foundations right
Duet is a phone-based personal agent for iPhone and Android, connected to Claude and positioned for small business owners and busy professionals. Think of the work you might reach for Claude Cowork to handle on your desktop, initiated from your phone instead.
The onboarding was excellent. It explained what Duet could do, what it could access, and how to get started. I had zero problems getting up and running. From the early TestFlight versions I used, the product felt unusually considered.
More importantly, it did not ask me to rebuild every connection. Duet inherits plugins and connectors from Claude. If your Claude setup already includes Gmail, Google, or Figma, those connections are available to the agent. That makes the starting point much more useful than an empty chat box.
Three interface choices stood out in actual use:
- Task lists made the agent’s work visible. I like being able to distinguish what I am doing from what the agent is doing.
- Artifacts had a dedicated place in the experience. Duet could already read artifacts on my Claude account, so I arrived with existing work available rather than an entirely blank workspace.
- Channels gave separate projects somewhere to live. I created a sales channel rather than putting every request into the main conversation.
The channels borrow a useful idea from Slack: a main conversation can coexist with focused spaces for particular work. Agent products are still sorting out whether their organizing unit should be a chat, thread, project, or something else. Channels were an understandable choice here.
The catch is that good organization solves only part of the problem. I could see where the work belonged. That did not guarantee I would come back when it was ready.
Inbox triage and ticket shopping exposed the follow-through problem
My first request was basic: go through my email and Slack and figure out what was happening.
Duet produced a few things, but the priorities and context did not seem right. It was okay, rather than exceptional. This is an important distinction for anyone evaluating an assistant: finding activity is easier than understanding which activity deserves your attention.
I did not have a precise prompt or a scored benchmark to share from this test. The result was my judgment as the person who knew the underlying work. If you adapt this evaluation, compare the agent’s proposed priorities with your own before letting it determine your day. That is a suggested testing method, not something Duet demonstrated automatically.
The more revealing task was shopping for Warriors tickets. I wanted to see the Warriors play the Pacers at a noon game, which meant I could take my kids. I have been asking my agents to shop for tickets and shoes, so this was a familiar, practical evaluation.
I kicked off the request while I was a passenger on the way to dinner. Then I waited. Eventually, I forgot about it. By the time I returned, my attention had shifted.
There is no completed ticket purchase to report here. The meaningful outcome was the broken interaction: Duet tracked the task, but it did not bring me back to resolve it.
That pattern became more noticeable when I gave it several requests. It could kick off individual threads for email, a deck, edits, or social work, but those threads could take 10-plus minutes to finish, return, or ask for permissions. Because the agent was quiet, I forgot about the open threads.
I cannot tell you whether I had missed a notification setting. I explicitly wondered about that during the review. What I can say is that after setting it up and trying the first few tasks, I did not experience the kind of useful prompting that would pull me back in.
A morning briefing does not solve this for me. I already get briefings from other agents. The useful interruption is more specific: the work is ready, a permission is blocking progress, or there is a decision I need to make. That is the behavior I wanted, not an observed Duet capability in this test.
Speed matters more when the agent is your conversation partner
I liked Duet’s interface responsiveness. The phone experience itself felt zippy. The work behind the interface was the slow part.
That distinction matters. A polished app can still feel slow if every meaningful exchange requires a long wait for the model or agent to finish.
I use Codex throughout the day, and one reason I stay engaged is that I can keep moving to the next step. Speed is also the feature I especially appreciate in Meta Muse. A responsive agent makes it easier to stay in a working rhythm.
With Duet, the delay reduced my willingness to work synchronously. An agent can be available around the clock and still feel unavailable at the moment I need it. I may choose the more responsive option even if I think it does a somewhat worse job, because it keeps the work moving.
This is not a measured head-to-head model comparison. It is a description of what made me reach for one product over another. Intelligence, latency, and follow-through combine into the experience of reliability.
The missing desktop experience compounded that problem. At the time of my test, Duet did not show up in the desktop app. I do not want to spend my working day on my phone while I am at my computer or in meetings.
The handoff I want is straightforward: start something asynchronously on my phone, then finish it at my desk. Muse’s desktop app supports my habit of returning to that agent. Grok Bot also stays present in my working environment. Duet’s mobile-only experience left it disconnected from where I do much of my work.
The lesson for evaluating an agent is to test the return trip. Starting a task from a phone is only half the workflow. Where will you review the result, answer a question, and approve the next step?
Sales work was useful; brand and local skills did not carry over cleanly
The business tasks were a better fit for Duet’s existing connections.
When I asked it to look at my sales pipeline, it already had access to Slack, email, and our CRM. It could pull in that data pretty quickly. That was a concrete advantage: I did not need to assemble and paste all the inputs myself.
I also had it create a deck in Google Docs from my phone. The deck was not bad. For an everyday business user who wants to generate a sales deck or document on the go, that could be useful.
My disappointment was design fidelity. I have a high bar, and I wanted it to use Figma and match our design, including fonts. It did not do that. The result met a more basic standard than the one I had in mind.
The copyable part is the connected starting point: use the business systems the agent can already access to produce a draft. The added guidance is to make the output destination and visual requirements explicit, then inspect the result. This test does not establish that a connected Figma account means Duet will choose Figma or reproduce your brand correctly.
The launch-video request exposed a different boundary. I had been making launch videos for ChatPRD in Claude and wanted to create that kind of work from Duet on my phone.
Duet did not ingest all my local skills. The setup behind those videos therefore did not simply travel with me into the mobile product.
I suspected I would need to publish those skills as Claude plugins for Duet to access them. That was a proposed next step, not a fix I completed and verified during the episode.
This is worth checking before moving any established workflow to a new agent surface. Existing artifacts, connected services, and local skills are different kinds of context. In my test, some carried over elegantly; others did not. Access to the same account did not mean access to every ingredient that made the original workflow work.
Channels organize solo work. They do not make an agent a teammate
Duet’s channels felt familiar because they resembled Slack. But they did not provide the multiplayer sharing that makes Slack useful to my team.
I am a small business owner, which should make me a good fit for this product. I am also working regularly with about five humans. I do not need a full enterprise deployment, but I do need ways to share work and agents with those people.
I have been moving more of my Grok Bot usage toward team agents deployed in Slack. Duet, in this test, was clearly a single-player agent. Organizing my own conversations into channels did not remove that limitation.
That changes the buying—or habit-building—decision. A solo professional may care most about access to email, documents, and a convenient mobile interface. A small team may care more about whether an agent’s work can become shared work without one person relaying everything.
My verdict: Duet is worth trying for Claude users who want a polished, phone-first assistant for individual business tasks. The inherited connections, visible task tracking, and accessible artifacts are worth copying. Generating a serviceable business draft from your phone is a real use case.
It did not earn a place as my primary agent in this test. Slow task completion, quiet follow-up, the missing desktop experience, and the lack of team sharing kept it below tools already embedded in my day.
Human judgment still mattered at every consequential point: deciding whether inbox priorities were right, whether a deck met the brand standard, whether a workflow had the skills it needed, and whether the agent actually helped finish the job. The standard is not how elegantly an agent ac

title: Inside Reddit Proto: Real Data, Constrained Prototypes, and a Better Handoff
summary: Reddit’s Blair Metcalf shows how an internal prototyping harness gives designers and product managers realistic data, design-system guardrails, and a more deliberate path from Figma to production-shaped code.
body:
Inside Reddit Proto: Real Data, Constrained Prototypes, and a Better Handoff
Reddit’s Blair Metcalf shows how an internal prototyping harness gives designers and product managers realistic data, design-system guardrails, and a more deliberate path from Figma to production-shaped code.
Featuring Blair Metcalf · Principal UX Engineer at Reddit
Claire Vo
Watch or listen to the full episode
Episode chapters
6 chapters
- 2:26A prototyping harness that hides GitWhy Reddit built its own launchpad and which design-system, navigation, device, and persona controls builders receive.
- 5:48Signed-in data and targeted Cursor annotationsBlair demonstrates a search prototype grounded in personalized Reddit data and annotations that become specific code-edit requests.
- 11:21Sharing, discovery, and leadership alignmentHow internally public prototypes support reviews, what adoption looks like, and why a dashboard of about seven hundred prototypes needs better discovery.
- 15:48Figma to feature capsule, PRD, and reviewed codeThe production-oriented handoff uses Figma, a design-system map, a custom MCP, and a PRD before code is generated in a sibling repository.
- 22:51Visually verifying the design-system source of truthBlair explains why the team built an inspectable map of tokens, components, surfaces, and workflows to verify the harness and MCP.
- 26:03Creative side projects and getting AI unstuckTeam playing cards lead into Blair’s prompting advice: step outside narrow project context and restate the facts and intent at a higher level.
Workflows from this episode
- Create a Realistic Prototype with Live Data in Reddit Proto
- Generate a Draft Pull Request from a Figma Design with Reddit Proto
All workflows
Episode outline
The most unusual thing about Reddit’s prototyping system is that you can sign in and see your own Reddit data inside a design that hasn’t shipped.
That changes the review. A search prototype has to return something relevant. A personalized feed can’t hide behind carefully selected placeholder posts. A leader can click around with their own account and discover whether the idea makes sense to them.
It also creates an important distinction: realistic enough to evaluate is not the same as ready for production.
Blair Metcalf, Principal UX Engineer at Reddit, demonstrates both sides of that boundary in Reddit Proto, the company’s internal prototyping harness. Designers and product managers can build within Reddit’s components and UX patterns, share working prototypes, and test ideas with signed-in data. Getting code toward production is a separate, more deliberate process involving Figma, a generated PRD, a custom MCP, and engineering review.
The useful lesson is how much work Reddit has put into deciding what the AI should already know—and what the person using it should never have to configure.
Hide Git, expose the decisions that matter
Reddit Proto starts with a desktop launchpad. A designer or product manager names a project and loads the boilerplate. The app handles cloning the repository and establishing the starting point; the user doesn’t need to reason about branches or repository setup before trying an idea.
They can work in their preferred IDE. Cursor is the tool Blair demonstrates for applying AI-generated changes.
The scaffold contains Reddit’s design system, components, UX patterns, and examples of features. As the team adds useful capabilities, those can become part of the shared starting point. Rather than asking every new prototype to rediscover how Reddit works, the team maintains that context centrally.
The controls exposed to the builder are product decisions:
- Turn features on or off.
- Change the device and theme.
- Test different user states, including moderator status.
- Enable or prevent navigation.
- Switch from mocked data to signed-in data.
Preventing navigation is a particularly good detail. In a working prototype, an enthusiastic reviewer can click straight out of the experience you intended to discuss. Constraining navigation lets the builder say, effectively: this is the decision we’re reviewing today.
The principle worth copying is selective simplicity. Hide the mechanics that repeatedly trip people up, but expose the controls that help them test a product hypothesis. A blank chat box over an unfamiliar repository would make the user do much more of that work.
Give the prototype real data—and give Cursor a precise target
Blair’s search example begins with annotations inside the prototype. He writes:
“Make relevant typeaheads trending recent communities, et cetera.”
He adds an overall direction:
“Using the signed-in Reddit data and real typeaheads as user types in the search box.”
Then he sends the annotations to Cursor. That action writes a file; in Cursor, he gives the instruction “Apply annotations.”
The useful part is what accompanies the request. The annotation carries the location in the code, the targeted element, the requested change, and the broader direction. Cursor is receiving a grounded edit request rather than being asked to infer which search box, component, or surface the user meant.
Blair says this lets builders target a surface, composite, or component while using Reddit’s design tokens and components. He also demonstrates the simpler case of selecting an element and asking to make it italic.
The search experiment was something he had been playing with before the recording, and he was surprised it worked. Searching for “How I AI” recognized the podcast; Blair describes the flow as pulling real data, sending it to an LLM, and ranking it. He does not identify the model or show a detailed evaluation of the search quality.
That distinction matters. The demonstration establishes that a realistic search interaction can be assembled and explored quickly. It does not establish that the ranking is production-ready. Blair explicitly says he hadn’t spent time on the design; a designer could then develop the landing experience, typeaheads, and results.
His reason for using signed-in data is pragmatic: Reddit is personalized. A mocked Figma experience may look polished and still feel irrelevant to the person reviewing it. Their own data gives them a reason to exercise the feature more seriously.
For another team, the adaptable pattern is to connect a prototype to representative, authorized data through a controlled path. This is an internal, privacy-controlled workflow—not a recommendation to give arbitrary prototypes unrestricted production access. The episode demonstrates the capability, not the underlying permission architecture.
Seven hundred prototypes create a discovery problem
Reddit Proto handles deployment as well as project creation. Blair describes the infrastructure, which uses Kubernetes, as “basically like an internal Vercel.” Builders can share a URL internally, including through Slack. He also demonstrates a security-gated sharing route and installed PWAs that can be used on a phone.
The prototypes are public within Reddit by default. That is useful for visibility, but it is also a product choice with consequences: when asked about private projects, Blair acknowledges that the team needs to add that capability.
At the time of the conversation, the dashboard held about seven hundred prototypes. A list of that size no longer works particularly well. The team is developing a searchable console to help people discover work by person, area, tag, team, and prototype type, with iOS and Android among the directions discussed.
Here, it is important to separate what exists from what is coming. Leadership already reviews working prototypes, clicks through them, and gives feedback live or in Slack. Live commenting on prototypes, comments that could trigger another build, and additional console commenting are described as work in progress.
Blair reports “100% adoption in UX and product,” across over 150 people, with a nearly even mix of design and product. Some of the strongest prototypers have been a visual designer and an animator. His explanation is that they are good directors: they carry substantial context, can describe what they want, and are willing to try things that might fail.
When I ask where the impact is strongest, Blair’s answer is “instant alignment.” Real data and familiar components reduce the distracting objections that can consume a design review. People can focus on whether the feature should exist and how it should behave.
That is a reported organizational benefit, not a measured cycle-time result. But it is a more useful target than counting how quickly someone can generate a screen.
The route toward production still runs through a PRD
The handoff is where the demo becomes more cautious—and more interesting.
Can a team take prototype code and send it to production? Blair calls that “the big puzzle piece.” Reddit has experimented with prototype-to-production flows, but the demonstrated route starts from high-fidelity Figma.
Using a sample feature for saving posts to folders, he copies a Figma location into a launchpad flow and creates what the team calls a feature capsule. Figma MCP analyzes the selected frames and components, while Reddit’s system maps that design to known production components and incorporates lessons from CI reviews and engineering feedback.
An intermediate output is a PRD. It includes the user goal, acceptance criteria, details about the work, and links back to Figma. The user reviews and confirms the interpretation, accepts the document, saves it locally, and sends it to Cursor.
Blair says they tried a broader “kitchen sink” approach and then narrowed back toward high-fidelity UI. That is a useful constraint to preserve. The system is not presented as reliably converting every aspect of a product idea into a complete implementation.
The PRD carries weight because it was already the handoff to engineering. It makes scope, goals, and workflows explicit before the agent starts writing code. This is where my enthusiasm for a written specification remains intact: an interactive artifact can show behavior, but it doesn’t automatically communicate every boundary of the work.
The code is written into a sibling repository to keep production clean. It can iterate there and produce a draft PR. That PR gets reviewed and, as Blair emphasizes, may or may not go through.
The copyable pattern is a checkpoint between interpretation and implementation. Ask a person to approve what the system believes it is building before treating generated code as progress.
The design-system map needs inspection, too
Behind that handoff is a substantial grounding effort. Reddit started with the Reddit Proto design system, read production code, and mapped the two. Blair names CodeConnect as part of connecting the design assets and implementation.
He shows a visualization covering tokens, components, surfaces, and journeys across RPL, Reddit Product Language. A token can be mapped into Figma, iOS, GitHub, and the prototyping GitHub. The visualization can also reveal differences in literal token values across platforms.
The custom MCP, shown as Proto MCP Ultra, uses that knowledge to find tokens, components, and examples for generating production-shaped code. Its quality depends on the map—and on feedback from attempts to use it.
Blair describes the process plainly: start with a map, try, fail, iterate, and refine the MCP using engineering feedback. Some submitted PRs pass CI review; others do not. Those outcomes improve the system.
The visualization exists because earlier attempts left people asking a basic question: what is actually in the harness? Being able to inspect an avatar’s colors, surfaces, and workflows gives the team a way to verify coverage rather than assume it.
This is one of the strongest ideas in the episode. If an agent is supposed to use your design system, you need a way to inspect its source of truth. Putting documentation within reach is different from verifying that the required relationships are repr
